description:
Start with a real project

Pick a category, market and format before collecting examples. Save the date and why an ad caught your attention.

Review the first version

Compare the first frame, the offer and the action each ad asks for. Group examples by pattern, such as a product demo or a customer question.

Check the final result

Write your own script using the underlying idea and your own images. Measure your own campaign results before drawing conclusions.

Frequently asked questions

Does a long-running ad prove it made money?

Treat duration as a research clue. Your own performance data is needed to judge results for your campaign.

Browse related tools on [SEOGBTools](https://seogbtools.com/).

Compare the ad openings and write your own test

Choose one category and collect several ads from the same market and format. Write down the offer, the first thing viewers see, and the action each ad asks them to take. For a desk lamp, one ad may open with glare on a monitor. Another might show how the lamp fits on a narrow desk. Those openings test different needs even when the product is similar.

Choose one idea that fits your own product and make two openings using footage you own. Keep the offer and landing page consistent across the test if the goal is to compare the openings. Use your own campaign results to decide which one performs better. An ad library gives examples of creative work, while your results show how your own audience responds.

Does an ad's long run reveal its profit?

Treat the run length as a reason to look closer. Profit depends on costs and sales data that an ad example alone cannot establish.

**Public keyword candidates** BigSpy group buy, competitor ad research, ad library, creative testing.

What to look for in a BigSpy ad search

Start with one product category and one advertising question. A skincare team might ask how brands explain a simple morning routine. A software company might ask how ads show a task getting done in under a minute. A narrow question makes it easier to compare examples that are aimed at similar buyers.

Where the search interface provides them, use platform, market, date, and format filters to narrow your examples. Review several advertisers and keep only the examples that match your question. A short video aimed at first-time buyers has a different job from a reminder ad for people who already visited the shop. Record the likely audience and offer separately from the visual style.

Break each ad into parts you can test

Record the opening line, the first thing a viewer sees, the proof offered, and the action the ad asks the viewer to take. For a video, note when the product becomes visible. For an image, check whether you can identify the offer without reading the caption. Pay attention to the first screen of the landing page where it is publicly available. The ad may make sense only because that page explains the price or terms.

Imagine a desk lamp ad starts with a dark desk and then shows the lamp lighting one work area. The transferable idea is to demonstrate the change in one shot. If your own product is a monitor light, you could show a real workspace and film how the light falls on the desk. Use your own footage, copy, brand colors, and claims. A clear demonstration gives you something to test without borrowing another advertiser's work.

Compare BigSpy with other ad research options

Use the same brand or topic when comparing BigSpy, Meta Ad Library, and TikTok Creative Center. Start with the channel you actually advertise on. Check how easily you can find a relevant creative, verify the advertiser, and record the date. If you are comparing paid tools such as Minea or AdSpy, check which platforms and filters the plan you are considering includes. Platform coverage and limits can change.

An ad library shows examples that were captured or made available. A visible ad can suggest a format worth studying. It cannot tell you the advertiser's actual margins, conversion rate, or reason for running the ad. Even if several versions look similar, the advertiser could be testing audiences, markets, or placements that you cannot see.

Plan a creative test from the research

Choose one change at a time. For example, keep the same offer and landing page and compare two openings. One can show the problem first. The other can show the finished result first. Use the same campaign goal and compare results over a period that gives both ads a fair chance. Look at the metric that matches your goal. A strong video view rate can help you understand attention, while checkout events are closer to a purchase goal.

Before choosing BigSpy group buy access, check what the listing includes for search limits, ad platforms, and saving examples. If you are preparing work for clients, use your own files to store the strategy and keep their private campaign figures out of shared research notes.

Build an ad research brief before you open BigSpy

Write a sentence that explains the decision you need to make. “Which product demonstration should we film for our new travel backpack?” is specific enough to guide a search. “Find winning ads” leaves you guessing about what to save and what a win means. Add your market, target buyer, likely channel, and the action you want someone to take after seeing the ad. Keep the brief close while you search so you can reject interesting examples that are outside your project.

Imagine you run a shop that sells a carry-on backpack. You want a short video for buyers who travel with one bag. Look for brands showing how much a bag holds, how it fits under a seat, and how quickly someone can reach a passport. Those are three questions the ads can answer. Save a few examples for each question. A fourth group could cover offers such as free shipping, but only if your team can actually offer it.

A clear brief also helps you decide which competitors to study. Direct competitors sell a similar backpack. Other advertisers may serve the same traveler with packing cubes, laptop sleeves, or luggage. Those examples can help you see ways to demonstrate an item or answer a buyer's question. Keep them in a separate part of your notes so the team knows which examples compete for the same sale and which were collected for their format.

Search by product, buyer problem, and advertiser

Try several ways to find the same category. A brand search can show how one advertiser presents different products. A product phrase such as carry-on backpack can surface a mix of sellers. A phrase such as “fits under the seat” can help you find ads focused on a buyer's problem. The results from one search may be too narrow to show the range of approaches available.

Use a date range that matches your question. Recent examples help when you are planning a campaign for the current season. Older examples can show how brands explained a similar offer before a previous holiday. Compare dates against the promotion you see in the ad. A limited-time discount may be over even if the creative still appears in a library.

Save the wording you used for each search and the filters you applied. If you later notice that all examples came from one market or one platform, repeat the search with a more useful scope. Keeping the date and filter settings also makes the research easier to update. A colleague should be able to understand how you arrived at a sample without needing to reproduce every click.

Build a balanced sample of competitor ads

Collect several examples from different advertisers before drawing a conclusion. If your sample has ten ads from one brand, you may be seeing one team's style over and over. Add examples from a small shop, an established brand, and a seller with a different price point if they address the same buyer question. Look for repeated approaches and for important questions that few ads answer.

Avoid comparing an ad for a premium product directly with an ad for a budget product without noting the price difference. The premium brand may spend more time explaining materials and warranty. A budget advertiser may lead with price and convenience. Both ads can be relevant to your category, but the offer needs to fit the product and the audience you are trying to reach.

Keep rejected examples out of the main collection and record common reasons for dropping them. For example, an ad might show a different item from the one named in the caption, a product you cannot ship, or a language you cannot review well enough to judge the copy. After the first pass, the remaining examples should be small enough for someone else to review in one meeting.

Turn a scroll-through into a useful creative review

Use the same notes for every ad. Record the advertiser, channel, observed date, product, offer, format, hook, proof, and call to action. Add the public destination if it still works. Write the strongest detail in your own words. “Packs three days of clothes in one continuous shot” tells a designer more than “good video.” If the ad uses an animation or a customer quote, note what role that element plays in the message.

For a video, watch it once without sound and once with sound. Check whether the item and its benefit are clear before the voice begins. Then note whether the voice adds facts, explains a step, or simply repeats what is already on screen. If your team uses captions, check whether a viewer can read the key line while the product is visible. These observations can guide your own script and shot list.

For a static image, look at the small version first. The image needs to make sense in a feed, where the viewer may not expand it. Note whether the product stands out, whether the offer can be read, and how much visual space the image gives to each. Use these observations to choose a layout for your own brand. A research note should describe how the example works so the team can produce fresh work.

Example of a BigSpy research session for a backpack shop

Start with the packing question. Find short product demos that show an empty bag, the items going inside, and the final size of the bag. Record how quickly each ad answers the buyer's main question. One might show all the items on a table before the first cut. Another might start with a full bag and then open it. Both are worth testing because they put the same information in a different order.

Next, look for a size and fit demonstration. If your bag meets the dimensions stated on your own product page, film it beside a tape measure or inside a test frame. Use your actual bag and show what happens when the front pocket is full. Avoid making an airline-specific promise unless you can support it. The proof needs to match the claims and dimensions the buyer will see after clicking.

Create two original scripts using what you learned. In the first, show the items on a bed and put them into the bag. In the second, open with the bag sliding under a seat in a controlled setup, then show what is inside. Keep the product page, offer, and call to action consistent so the opening is the main change. List the props, location, product features, and shots for each script. Give the filming team one sentence that describes the buyer's question each video answers.

After the test, compare results against the campaign goal. If the opening earns more video views but fewer people click, check whether the middle of the ad explains why the product is worth a closer look. If more people click but sales stay flat, inspect the landing page for gaps such as unclear dimensions, shipping costs, or stock availability. Keep the research notes and your actual campaign results in the same project so the next brief can build on what you learned.

Review the landing page and offer together

An ad and its landing page share the job of explaining what a buyer gets. Open the public page and see whether the main product, offer, and next step match the ad. A product demonstration may lead to a specific item page, while a sale announcement may lead to a collection. Record which route the advertiser chose and what the first screen shows. If the destination is unavailable, mark it as unavailable and move on.

For your own campaign, check that a discount or bundle mentioned in the ad can be found on the destination page. If an offer depends on a code or a minimum order, explain the terms where the buyer can see them. A mismatch can cost clicks and make an ad test hard to interpret. Test the page on the device your audience is likely to use and follow the path from the first screen to the point where the buyer can act.

Look beyond the offer to the proof. An ad might promise that a bag fits a specific laptop size. The page should list the actual compartment dimensions and help a buyer check their device. If the buyer has to search through reviews to find the answer, update the product details. Competitor research can help uncover the question. Your own measurements and photos should supply the answer.

Organize your examples for a small team

Give each example one purpose in your working collection. Label it as a demonstration, comparison, testimonial format, or offer example. Add a note that says why it belongs there. Avoid keeping dozens of screenshots with no context. A short folder of examples linked to clear decisions is easier to use when a designer or editor starts work.

End the review with a small list of decisions. Choose two angles worth testing, a format the team can produce, and one idea to leave for later. Assign someone to check that the planned copy matches the product and someone to review the final edit. Save the research date and a link to the original example where available so the team can revisit it if the campaign changes.

Does a long-running ad mean it is profitable?

It means you observed the example across a period or saw a record that spans those dates. An advertiser may keep an ad available for different reasons. Use it as a reason to study the message and format. Use your own campaign and sales data to judge performance on your offer.

Can I use an ad spy tool for a service business?

Yes. Search for examples that answer buyer questions about the service, such as what is included, where it is offered, or how booking works. Look at how ads show real work or explain the next step. Use your own photos, service details, and proof when you build the campaign.

How often should I refresh a creative collection?

Review it when you change your offer, enter a new market, or prepare a new batch of ads. Keep older examples that still help answer a clear question. Remove links that no longer work and update notes when the offer or channel changes. A dated collection is easier to maintain than a growing folder with no record of when anything was found.
